source.title: Sparse Autoencoders enable Robust and Interpretable Fine-tuning of CLIP models
source.authors: Fabian Morelli; Arnas Uselis; Ankit Sonthalia; S. Oh

page_placements.theme: SAE transfer depends on representational alignment

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports SAE reconstruction-error measurements, but does not investigate the structure or functional effects of dark matter, or whether its properties change across SAE sizes.
record.gate_note: Tables 2 and 7 report FVU for a zero-shot-trained SAE applied to different CLIP representations. These measure reconstruction error but do not test any listed version's specific claim about the error. The architecture ablation reports downstream accuracy, not reconstruction-error properties.
record.test_reason: The study uses a Top-K SAE trained on zero-shot CLIP vision representations as a regularizer for fine-tuning and reports downstream accuracy. Its FVU numbers measure how well a fixed SAE reconstructs drifted representations. None tests linear predictability of the error, scaling of error across SAE sizes, pathological loss effects, a linear/nonlinear split, functional loss without the error term, or training-artifact explanations. The residual penalty (Eq. 6) forces fine-tuning updates into the decoder span, which uses the SAE as a tool rather than studying its error. T4 (uses the SAE as a tool) fits better than T6.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that constraining fine-tuning to a zero-shot SAE's feature span gives state-of-the-art robustness and interpretable feature re-weighting. They also say gains over plain L2 regularization are marginal; the main benefit is finer control and interpretability.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains a Top-K SAE on zero-shot CLIP vision representations and uses it to regularize fine-tuning; it does not study the dark-matter error decomposition or compare its structure across SAE sizes.
record.method_sensitivity: SAE-FT downstream performance varies with SAE architecture: the paper reports OOD benchmark sensitivity to the number of active features and dictionary multiplier, with regularization hyperparameters held fixed.

fits_no_version.finding: A fixed SAE trained on zero-shot CLIP has FVU 0.22 in distribution. FVU rises above 1 on standard fine-tuned representations and is 0.65 on WiSE-FT. It stays near 0.23–0.25 under L2 regularization or SAE-FT.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A fixed SAE's reconstruction error rises sharply under fine-tuning-induced representational drift.

record.problems: The paper does not test the dark-matter claim's specified properties. FVU is reported for selected representation conditions, without uncertainty estimates for those FVU values.
record.rows_left_out: None of the reported FVU table entries were left out. Figure 2 is not separately extracted because its FVU curve is shown graphically and the text provides only a qualitative description, while the tabulated FVU results are recorded above.

untested.parts: Linear predictability of the SAE error from the input activation.
Error-norm predictability across SAE sizes; persistence of error with scale. The architecture ablation reports only downstream accuracy, not FVU.
Loss effect of splicing in SAE reconstructions versus random errors of the same size.
Split of the error into linear and nonlinear parts, and how each responds to dictionary learning.
Loss of behaviour in SAE-based analyses when the error term is dropped.
Whether dark matter is an artifact of SAE training, or shrinks with better architectures or end-to-end training.

record.verdict_notes: The record's relation and tranche were changed from discusses/T6 to uses_without_test/T4, because the SAE is central to the method but its error is never analysed. The paper's text says FVU > 1 means the SAE is worse than a zero-vector baseline. Appendix B defines FVU against a constant-mean predictor, so this is a minor wording inconsistency in the paper.

versions.untested_parts: Whether a large share of SAE error is linearly predictable from the input activation.
Whether per-token error norms are predictable across SAE sizes, larger SAEs fail on the same contexts, or error persists with scale.
Whether replacing activations with SAE reconstructions harms model loss more than same-size random errors.
Whether linear and nonlinear error components differ in the proposed ways or respond differently to dictionary learning.
Whether SAE-feature analyses lose model behavior when the error term is omitted.
Whether dark matter is primarily a training artifact or shrinks with improved SAE architectures or end-to-end training.

relation.reason: The study discusses SAE reconstruction error and constrains changes in the residual during fine-tuning. It does not use any listed dark-matter claim as a tool.

tranche.reason: The study uses an SAE as a fine-tuning regularizer, but neither tests nor relies on any listed dark-matter finding. Its FVU measurements characterize reconstruction under representational drift, a related but different construct.

source_check.notes: None of the five FVU measurements tests V1–V6. Section 4 describes the FVU baseline as zero-vector prediction, whereas Appendix B formally defines it as prediction of the empirical mean; the recorded baseline follows Appendix B.
